title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April-May 2026.
abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

title: Immunogenicity of Hantavirus and evaluation of vaccine protective efficacy: A comparative neutralizing antibody study of vaccine strains and representative epidemic strains from selected provinces in China.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.

title_zh: 汉坦病毒 的免疫原性和 疫苗 保护功效的评估:疫苗 株与中国部分省份代表性流行株的中和抗体比较研究。
source_body_en: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantavirus (HV) remains a significant public health burden in the world. HFRS bivalent inactivated vaccine (HFRSbiv) with Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) strains isolated 20 years ago have been used in key HFRS endemic provinces in China for HFRS prevention. After decades of effective implementation of comprehensive prevention and control measures, HFRS has entered a stage of epidemic fluctuation at low-level in China. However, the continuous transmission of the virus among rodent host animals may lead to dynamic changes in genetic diversity and immunogenicity of the virus, which may affect the pathogenic mechanism of the virus and the protective effect of vaccines. It is necessary to carry out timely monitoring and evaluation of the immunogenicity of HV. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: A panel of sera was established by screening serum samples from HFRS patients at convalescent phase and individuals who had received standardized immunization with HFRSbiv. Neutralizing antibody titers against HTNV vaccine strain 84FLi, SEOV vaccine strain L99, and three representative epidemic strains from different genotypes (HTNV: SX26, SEOV: LN03 and FJ-17) were measured using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based microneutralization test (MN-ELISA). HV-neutralizing antibodies were detected from all the selected serum samples. Among HFRS patients, 47.92% (23/48) were identified as HTNV infection, 27.08% (13/48) were with SEOV infection, and 25% (12/48) were untypable. There is a significant difference in the titers of neutralizing antibodies against vaccine strains and epidemic strains detected in the serum samples. For HTNV, both patient and vaccinee sera exhibited significantly higher geometric mean titer (GMT) against vaccine strain 84FLi than against epidemic strain SX26 (1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04, P < 0.001; 1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37, P < 0.05, respectively). For SEOV, patient sera showed significantly lower GMT against vaccine strain L99 than against epidemic strain LN03 (1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71, P < 0.01), and vaccinee sera showed significantly lower GMT against L99 than against epidemic strain FJ-17 (1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71, P < 0.001). Significant immunogenicity heterogeneity was observed between SEOV epidemic strains LN03 and FJ-17. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: The genetic diversity and immunogenicity of HV, which causes HFRS, have certain geographical regional characteristics. The levels of cross neutralizing antibodies induced by infection of HV from different genotypes may vary significantly, but still provide sufficient cross protection. The HFRSbiv currently used in China could induce broad neutralizing antibody, the cross-protective efficacy might vary against different circulating strains and genotypes. It is of great significance to strengthen the monitoring of genetic characteristics of regional specific circulating viral strains, regularly evaluate the matching degree between vaccine protection effectiveness and epidemic strains, predict and evaluate the transmission and pathogenic risks of HV, and timely optimize HFRS prevention and control strategies and measures.
abstract_zh: 背景:由汉坦病毒(HV) 引起的 肾综合征出血热 (HFRS) 仍然是世界上重大的公共卫生负担。20年前分离出的含有汉坦病毒(HTNV)和汉城病毒(SEOV)毒株的HFRS二价灭活疫苗(HFRSbiv)已在中国HFRS重点流行省份用于预防HFRS。经过几十年的综合防控措施的有效实施,我国HFRS已进入疫情低水平波动阶段。然而,该病毒在啮齿动物宿主动物中的持续传播可能会导致病毒遗传多样性和免疫原性的动态变化,从而可能影响病毒的致病机制和疫苗的保护作用。有必要及时开展HV免疫原性监测和评估。方法学/主要发现:通过筛选恢复期 HFRS 患者和接受 HFRSbiv 标准化免疫的个体的血清样本,建立了一组血清。使用基于酶联免疫吸附测定的微中和试验(MN-ELISA)测量了针对 HTNV 疫苗 株 84FLi、SEOV 疫苗 株 L99 和来自不同基因型的三种代表性流行株(HTNV:SX26、SEOV:LN03 和 FJ-17)的中和抗体滴度。从所有选定的血清样本中均检测到 HV 中和抗体。HFRS患者中,47.92%(23/48)被诊断为HTNV感染,27.08%(13/48)被诊断为SEOV感染,25%(12/48)未被分型。血清样本中检测到的疫苗株与流行株的中和抗体滴度存在显着差异。对于 HTNV,患者和疫苗接种者血清对 疫苗 84FLi 株的几何平均滴度 (GMT) 均显着高于流行株 SX26(分别为 1:386.08 vs. 1:223.04,P < 0.001;1:137.94 vs. 1:110.37,P < 0.05)。对于SEOV,患者血清针对疫苗毒株L99的GMT显着低于针对流行毒株LN03的GMT(1:177.02 vs. 1:297.71,P < 0.01),并且接种者血清针对L99的GMT显示显着低于针对流行毒株FJ-17的GMT(1:97.52 vs. 1:243.71,P < 0.01)。0.001)。SEOV 流行毒株 LN03 和 FJ-17 之间观察到显着的免疫原性异质性。结论/意义:导致 HFRS 的 HV 的遗传多样性和免疫原性具有一定的地理区域特征。不同基因型 HV 感染诱导的交叉中和抗体水平可能差异很大,但仍能提供足够的交叉保护。目前国内使用的HFRSbiv可诱导广泛的中和抗体,针对不同的流行毒株和基因型,交叉保护效果可能有所不同。加强地区特定流行病毒株遗传特征监测,定期评估疫苗防护效果与流行毒株的匹配程度,预测评估疫苗和HV致病风险,及时优化HFRS防控策略和措施具有重要意义。

title: The Potential Risk Factors of Hantavirus Transmission to Humans from Infected Rodents in Malaysia
abstract: Zoonotic hantavirus is a negative single-stranded RNA virus from the family Bunyaviridae which is known to cause two significant rodent-borne diseases in humans namely hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), affecting about 30 000 people worldwide each year. HFRS is a disease found endemically in Asia and Europe with case fatality rates varying from <1% to 12%, while HPS which has a higher mortality rate of approximately 40% occurs within the American continent. Many countries in Southeast Asia unaware the public health implication of Hantavirus infection despite favorable ecological conditions include rich rodent species diversity, urbanisation and high human-wildlife interface that serve as ecological condition that could support the virus persistence and transmission.Since humans serve as spillover hosts who are infected largely by inhalation of infected rodents’ excreta, it is crucial to fill in the research gap by identifying the risk factors for human hantavirus infection. This paper provides a review of the potential risk factors associated with hantavirus transmission to humans from infected rodents in Malaysia focusing on behavioral, occupational, urban, and environmental. Other pieces of knowledge such as hantavirus virological properties, the geographical distribution with its respective role as a reservoir, clinical features, and diagnostic challenges, particularly its propensity to be misclassified due to mimic symptom with dengue and leptospirosis. To effectively mitigate transmission, Malaysia must transition from a fragmented surveillance model to a proactive, integrated One Health framework that bridges the inter-governmental agencies through a unified data-sharing platform to monitor active viral strains and prevent localised spillover outbreaks.
journal: Pertanika Journal of Veterinary Medicine and Science

title_zh: 汉坦病毒 传播 对马来西亚受感染啮齿动物的潜在风险因素
source_body_en: Zoonotic hantavirus is a negative single-stranded RNA virus from the family Bunyaviridae which is known to cause two significant rodent-borne diseases in humans namely hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), affecting about 30 000 people worldwide each year. HFRS is a disease found endemically in Asia and Europe with case fatality rates varying from <1% to 12%, while HPS which has a higher mortality rate of approximately 40% occurs within the American continent. Many countries in Southeast Asia unaware the public health implication of Hantavirus infection despite favorable ecological conditions include rich rodent species diversity, urbanisation and high human-wildlife interface that serve as ecological condition that could support the virus persistence and transmission.Since humans serve as spillover hosts who are infected largely by inhalation of infected rodents’ excreta, it is crucial to fill in the research gap by identifying the risk factors for human hantavirus infection. This paper provides a review of the potential risk factors associated with hantavirus transmission to humans from infected rodents in Malaysia focusing on behavioral, occupational, urban, and environmental. Other pieces of knowledge such as hantavirus virological properties, the geographical distribution with its respective role as a reservoir, clinical features, and diagnostic challenges, particularly its propensity to be misclassified due to mimic symptom with dengue and leptospirosis. To effectively mitigate transmission, Malaysia must transition from a fragmented surveillance model to a proactive, integrated One Health framework that bridges the inter-governmental agencies through a unified data-sharing platform to monitor active viral strains and prevent localised spillover outbreaks.

title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
abstract: Abstract Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

title_zh: 安第斯山脉病毒谱系的分子 进化 导致最近的人类 暴发
source_body_en: Abstract Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak.
abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.
authors: International Consortium Investigating the M/V Hondius Outbreak

title: An NCG mouse model of Hantaan virus reveals systemic infection and organ-specific cellular tropism.
abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.

title_zh: 汉坦病毒的 NCG 小鼠模型揭示了全身感染和器官特异性细胞向性。
source_body_en: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) is primarily endemic across Eurasia, posing a severe threat of renal failure and mortality. The mechanisms of HTNV infection remain poorly understood, largely due to the lack of susceptible animal models. In this study, we established a systemic HTNV infection mouse model using highly immunodeficient NCG mice. Following viral inoculation, we assessed viral loads via quantitative RT-PCR and mapped cellular tropism and co-localization of HTNV with potential receptors using immunofluorescence staining. While histopathological lesions were subclinical, HTNV-infected NCG mice exhibited robust viremia and sustained viral replication across multiple organs, including the kidney, lung, spleen, reproductive organs, and liver. HTNV exhibited distinct organ-specific cellular tropism in vivo, predominantly targeting fibroblasts and interstitial cells of the renal collecting duct in the kidney, alveolar epithelial cells and macrophages in the lung, and broadly infecting multiple cell populations in the brain and ovary. Co-localization analyses indicated HTNV infection might be associated with distinct entry receptors across target organs: potentially ITGB1 and gC1qR in specific renal cells, and ITGB1 and ITGB2 in pulmonary AT1 cells and macrophages, respectively. These findings demonstrate that NCG mouse is a valuable in vivo model for studying HTNV replication and systemic dissemination.
abstract_zh: 由汉滩病毒 (HTNV) 引起的 肾综合征出血热 (HFRS) 主要在欧亚大陆流行,对肾衰竭和 死亡率 构成严重威胁。HTNV 感染的机制仍然知之甚少,很大程度上是由于缺乏易感动物模型。在这项研究中,我们使用高度免疫缺陷的NCG小鼠建立了系统性HTNV感染小鼠模型。病毒接种后,我们通过定量 RT-PCR 评估病毒载量,并使用免疫荧光染色绘制 HTNV 的细胞趋向性和与潜在受体的共定位。虽然组织病理学病变是亚临床的,但感染 HTNV 的 NCG 小鼠表现出强烈的病毒血症,并在多个器官(包括肾、肺、脾、生殖器官和肝脏)中持续病毒复制。HTNV在体内表现出独特的器官特异性细胞趋向性,主要针对肾脏中肾集合管的成纤维细胞和间质细胞,肺中的肺泡上皮细胞和巨噬细胞,并广泛感染大脑和卵巢中的多个细胞群。共定位分析表明,HTNV 感染可能与靶器官中不同的进入受体相关:特定肾细胞中可能存在 ITGB1 和 gC1qR,肺 AT1 细胞和巨噬细胞中分别存在 ITGB1 和 ITGB2。这些发现表明,NCG 小鼠是研究 HTNV 复制和系统传播的有价值的体内模型。

title: Persistent leukopenia masks hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) typically comes with fever, facial flushing, rash, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and leukocytosis. However, atypical manifestations may obscure diagnosis. A 30-year-old man with rodent exposure had high fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia, without overt renal dysfunction despite mild renal involvement in the form of proteinuria. Hantaan virus was confirmed by serology and RT-PCR. The patient recovered following ribavirin and supportive management. This case highlights that in HFRS-endemic regions, hantavirus infection should be suspected among patients with unexplained fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia rather than the typical leukocytosis, even without overt renal dysfunction.

title: Rat Hepatitis E Virus and Seoul Hantavirus in Pet Rats, Germany
abstract: Pet rats represent a reservoir of multiple zoonotic pathogens. We demonstrated that pet rats, previously confirmed to be Seoul orthohantavirus–infected and involved in human infections in Germany, were concurrently infected with rat hepatitis E virus. The high degree of rat hepatitis E virus sequence identity suggests a single incursion event.

title: Assessing the performance of time series prediction models for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across different high-risk areas in Shaanxi Province, China
abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a climate-sensitive disease. Existing forecasting models often overlook prefecture-level variations and environmental drivers. This study compares time series models incorporating environmental factors for prefecture-level HFRS prediction. Methods Monthly HFRS case counts and 14 environmental factors were collected from 2005 to 2023 in four typical prefecture-level cities, including Xi'an, Baoji, Xianyang, and Weinan. Core factors were determined via stepwise screening. We developed four time series models: univariate seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) and long short-term memory (LSTM), alongside their multivariate counterparts with exogenous variables (SARIMAX and LSTMX). Specifically, multivariate models incorporated screened environmental drivers, whereas univariate models relied solely on historical epidemic data. Model robustness was further assessed by rolling-origin validation across three test years (2021−2023), in which the entire modeling pipeline was re-executed within each training window, and the sensitivity of LSTMX performance to the covariate-selection strategy was quantified. Results The predictive value of environmental covariates for HFRS forecasting varied by city and evaluation context. In Xi'an and Baoji, the multivariate LSTMX model showed lower forecasting errors (Xi'an: R 2 = 0.976, RMSE decreased from 69.246 to 17.782; Baoji: R 2 = 0.950, RMSE decreased from 6.694 to 2.805). Conversely, in Xianyang and Weinan, univariate SARIMA yielded lower errors (R 2 = 0.940 and 0.889, respectively), and incorporating covariates did not reduce forecasting errors. Rolling-origin validation across 2021–2023 yielded a consistent ranking: LSTMX had the lowest mean RMSE in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models had lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the screened covariate set was the only strategy that never caused a severe loss of accuracy, whereas including all 14 environmental variables did not reduce errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Pairwise model differences were not statistically significant after Holm correction, and the city ranking changed when the models were refitted on the monthly crude incidence-rate scale; the rankings are therefore reported descriptively and are not interpreted as evidence of regional differences in environmental effects. Conclusions No single forecasting configuration was uniformly optimal across cities: LSTMX with lagged environmental factors yielded the lowest errors in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models yielded lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan; however, these pairwise differences did not reach statistical significance after Holm correction and changed under the incidence-rate scale. When extending these models to new settings, both univariate and covariate-enhanced configurations should be compared.

title_zh: 评估中国陕西省不同高风险地区 肾综合征出血热 时间序列预测模型的性能
source_body_en: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a climate-sensitive disease. Existing forecasting models often overlook prefecture-level variations and environmental drivers. This study compares time series models incorporating environmental factors for prefecture-level HFRS prediction. Methods Monthly HFRS case counts and 14 environmental factors were collected from 2005 to 2023 in four typical prefecture-level cities, including Xi'an, Baoji, Xianyang, and Weinan. Core factors were determined via stepwise screening. We developed four time series models: univariate seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) and long short-term memory (LSTM), alongside their multivariate counterparts with exogenous variables (SARIMAX and LSTMX). Specifically, multivariate models incorporated screened environmental drivers, whereas univariate models relied solely on historical epidemic data. Model robustness was further assessed by rolling-origin validation across three test years (2021−2023), in which the entire modeling pipeline was re-executed within each training window, and the sensitivity of LSTMX performance to the covariate-selection strategy was quantified. Results The predictive value of environmental covariates for HFRS forecasting varied by city and evaluation context. In Xi'an and Baoji, the multivariate LSTMX model showed lower forecasting errors (Xi'an: R 2 = 0.976, RMSE decreased from 69.246 to 17.782; Baoji: R 2 = 0.950, RMSE decreased from 6.694 to 2.805). Conversely, in Xianyang and Weinan, univariate SARIMA yielded lower errors (R 2 = 0.940 and 0.889, respectively), and incorporating covariates did not reduce forecasting errors. Rolling-origin validation across 2021–2023 yielded a consistent ranking: LSTMX had the lowest mean RMSE in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models had lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the screened covariate set was the only strategy that never caused a severe loss of accuracy, whereas including all 14 environmental variables did not reduce errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Pairwise model differences were not statistically significant after Holm correction, and the city ranking changed when the models were refitted on the monthly crude incidence-rate scale; the rankings are therefore reported descriptively and are not interpreted as evidence of regional differences in environmental effects. Conclusions No single forecasting configuration was uniformly optimal across cities: LSTMX with lagged environmental factors yielded the lowest errors in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models yielded lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan; however, these pairwise differences did not reach statistical significance after Holm correction and changed under the incidence-rate scale. When extending these models to new settings, both univariate and covariate-enhanced configurations should be compared.
abstract_zh: 背景 肾综合征出血热 (HFRS) 是一种气候敏感疾病。现有的预测模型常常忽视地级市的变化和环境驱动因素。本研究比较了纳入环境因素的地市级 HFRS 预测的时间序列模型。方法收集西安、宝鸡、咸阳、渭南4个典型地级市2005—2023年每月HFRS病例数和14个环境因素。通过逐步筛选确定核心因素。我们开发了四种时间序列模型:单变量季节性自回归积分移动平均线 (SARIMA) 和长短期记忆 (LSTM),以及具有外生变量的多元对应模型(SARIMAX 和 LSTMX)。具体来说,多变量模型纳入了筛选的环境驱动因素,而单变量模型仅依赖于历史流行病数据。通过三个测试年(2021−2023)的滚动源验证进一步评估了模型的稳健性,其中在每个训练窗口内重新执行整个建模流程,并量化了 LSTMX 性能对协变量选择策略的敏感性。结果 HFRS 预测的环境协变量的预测值因城市和评估背景而异。在西安和宝鸡,多元LSTMX模型显示出较低的预测误差(西安:R 2 = 0.976,RMSE从69.246下降到17.782;宝鸡:R 2 = 0.950,RMSE从6.694下降到2.805)。相反,在咸阳和渭南,单变量 SARIMA 产生的误差较低(R 2 分别 = 0.940 和 0.889),并且纳入协变量并没有减少预测误差。2021-2023 年的滚动原点验证得出了一致的排名:LSTMX 在西安和宝鸡的平均 RMSE 最低,而单变量模型在咸阳和渭南的误差较低。敏感性分析表明,筛选的协变量集是唯一不会造成准确性严重损失的策略,而包括所有 14 个环境变量并没有减少咸阳和渭南的误差。Holm修正后两两模型差异不具有统计学意义,模型在月度粗发病率率量表上重新拟合后城市排名发生变化;因此,排名是描述性报告的,并不被解释为环境影响区域差异的证据。结论 没有单一的预测配置在各个城市中都是一致最优的:具有滞后环境因素的 LSTMX 在西安和宝鸡产生的误差最低,而单变量模型在咸阳和渭南产生的误差较低;然而,这些成对差异在 Holm 校正后并未达到统计学显着性,并且在 发病率 速率量表下发生了变化。将这些模型扩展到新设置时,应比较单变量和协变量增强配置。

title: Immature Platelet Fraction in Viral Infections: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives
abstract: Background: Reticulated platelets, reported by modern hematology analyzers as the immature platelet fraction (IPF%) or the absolute immature platelet count (IPC), index thrombopoiesis and have been proposed as biomarkers in the thrombocytopenia of viral infection. Methods: This systematic review, conducted and reported following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261501412), examined how these parameters have been used across viral diseases. PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2000 to May 2025 for observational studies of adults with viral infection reporting IPF, IPC, or reticulated platelets, and methodological robustness was appraised with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. Results: Twenty-two studies were included and synthesized narratively. Applications differed by pathogen: in dengue, serial IPF increases consistently preceded platelet recovery, although proposed thresholds varied; in COVID-19, higher immature platelet parameters were associated with severity and mortality but were inconsistent after adjustment. Evidence in chronic hepatitis, HIV, hantavirus, and Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever was mainly pathophysiological, and data in critically ill patients were almost confined to COVID-19. Conclusions: Clinical value appears disease- and outcome-specific: serial IPF best predicts platelet recovery in dengue, whereas prognostic use in COVID-19 remains insufficiently validated. Analytical heterogeneity and the absence of transferable thresholds currently limit clinical implementation.

title_zh: 病毒感染中的未成熟血小板分数:当前应用和未来前景的系统回顾
source_body_en: Background: Reticulated platelets, reported by modern hematology analyzers as the immature platelet fraction (IPF%) or the absolute immature platelet count (IPC), index thrombopoiesis and have been proposed as biomarkers in the thrombocytopenia of viral infection. Methods: This systematic review, conducted and reported following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261501412), examined how these parameters have been used across viral diseases. PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2000 to May 2025 for observational studies of adults with viral infection reporting IPF, IPC, or reticulated platelets, and methodological robustness was appraised with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. Results: Twenty-two studies were included and synthesized narratively. Applications differed by pathogen: in dengue, serial IPF increases consistently preceded platelet recovery, although proposed thresholds varied; in COVID-19, higher immature platelet parameters were associated with severity and mortality but were inconsistent after adjustment. Evidence in chronic hepatitis, HIV, hantavirus, and Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever was mainly pathophysiological, and data in critically ill patients were almost confined to COVID-19. Conclusions: Clinical value appears disease- and outcome-specific: serial IPF best predicts platelet recovery in dengue, whereas prognostic use in COVID-19 remains insufficiently validated. Analytical heterogeneity and the absence of transferable thresholds currently limit clinical implementation.

title: Reverse Vaccinology Design of an Asian HLA-Targeted Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against HTNV Strain 76-118
abstract: HTNV remains a cause of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, particularly in Asia, while broadly available vaccines remain limited. This study developed an Asian HLA-targeted multi-epitope vaccine candidate against HTNV strain 76-118 using reverse vaccinology and immunoinformatics. RdRp, GPC, and N proteins were screened for cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL), helper T-lymphocyte (HTL), and linear B-cell epitopes using 42 representative Asian HLA alleles. Selected epitopes were evaluated for immunological and safety properties, followed by population coverage analysis, vaccine construction, immune simulation, structural modeling, molecular docking, 300 ns molecular dynamics simulation, MM-GBSA analysis, and in silico cloning. Twenty-five epitopes, comprising 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B-cell epitopes, were retained. Combined MHC class I and II predicted coverage averaged 95.15% across five regions and reached 99.29% in East Asia. Among four adjuvant-based constructs, the HBHA-containing vaccine was prioritized based on combined physicochemical and comparative immune-simulation characteristics. Docking with TLR4 yielded a predicted ΔG of −27.6 kcal mol−1, while trajectory-based MM-GBSA analysis produced a ΔGbind of −136.17 ± 3.14 kcal mol−1. Codon optimization achieved a CAI of 0.9640 and GC content of 52.27%. Collectively, these computational analyses identify the HBHA-based construct as a population-oriented HTNV vaccine candidate prioritized for subsequent experimental evaluation.

RdRp, GPC, and N proteins were screened for cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL), helper T-lymphocyte (HTL), and linear B-cell epitopes using 42 representative Asian HLA alleles. Selected epitopes were evaluated for immunological and safety properties, followed by population coverage analysis, vaccine construction, immune simulation, structural modeling, molecular docking, 300 ns molecular dynamics simulation, MM-GBSA analysis, and in silico cloning. Twenty-five epitopes, comprising 10 CTL, 10 HTL, and 5 B-cell epitopes, were retained. Combined MHC class I and II predicted coverage averaged 95.15% across five regions and reached 99.29% in East Asia. Among four adjuvant-based constructs, the HBHA-containing vaccine was prioritized based on combined physicochemical and comparative immune-simulation characteristics. Docking with TLR4 yielded a predicted ΔG of −27.6 kcal mol−1, while trajectory-based MM-GBSA analysis produced a ΔGbind of −136.17 ± 3.14 kcal mol−1. Codon optimization achieved a CAI of 0.9640 and GC content of 52.27%. Collectively, these computational analyses identify the HBHA-based construct as a population-oriented HTNV vaccine candidate prioritized for subsequent experimental evaluation.

full_text: BackgroundHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges.Case presentationA 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology.ConclusionSeoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management. Laboratory and imaging findingsInitial laboratory investigations showed a mixed acid-base disturbance, characterized by respiratory alkalosis with normal anion-gap (AnGap 2-10 mmol/L),hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and liver function injury. The most striking abnormality was profound thrombocytopenia (29 × 109/L); urinalysis revealed hematuria and proteinuria.Table 2 was revised to add serum amylase, lipase, serum triglyceride, serum urea, serum creatinine, sodium, potassium, hemoglobin values. Reticulocyte count was not tested in clinical practice; hemoglobin levels over serial time-points are presented to evaluate for bone-marrow suppression. Urine sediment examination did not demonstrate granular or hyaline casts. Serial urine output was prospectively recorded as part of intensive care monitoring; overall urine output remained adequate throughout hospitalization without anuria or oliguric renal failure. Mild anemia was observed (minimum hemoglobin 127 g/L).Serial changes in leukocytes, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, neutrophil and lymphocyte percentages, transaminases, platelets, albumin, and coagulation parameters are summarized in Table 2. The dynamic clinical, laboratory, imaging, and management course across hospitalization is summarized in the diagnostic timeline (Table 1).Table 1Diagnostic timeline.Time pointClinical manifestationsKey laboratory findingsImaging & pathogen testClinical management & decision-makingOne week before admissionLow-grade intermittent fever, lumbago; mild fatty liver; no pancreatic swelling or peripancreatic fluidDischarged; outpatient follow-up scheduled for liver function and HBV monitoring DiscussionThis case highlights a diagnostically challenging presentation in which Seoul orthohantavirus infection clinically and radiologically mimicked severe acute pancreatitis, underscoring the need to consider HFRS in the differential diagnosis of unexplained pancreatitis-like presentations (1). Acute pancreatitis is a recognized but rare complication of HFRS (2, 6), and its distinction from hantavirus-induced pancreatic involvement is notoriously difficult because of overlapping clinical and imaging features (9). The present case further illustrates that peripancreatic exudation and retroperitoneal fluid—hallmark findings of severe acute pancreatitis—can also result from the profound systemic capillary leakage and retroperitoneal edema characteristic of hantavirus infection (4, 5). In this context, marked thrombocytopenia, renal impairment with hematuria and proteinuria, and the absence of typical pancreatitis risk factors constituted pivotal clues that prompted consideration of an alternative etiology (9). Moreover, the normal pancreatic enzyme levels observed here demonstrate that biochemical markers alone cannot reliably exclude HFRS in suspected pancreatitis (10).It should be acknowledged that severe acute pancreatitis itself may produce thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction secondary to systemic inflammation. However, several features argued against primary acute pancreatitis in this patient: thrombocytopenia was already present at initial presentation as a critical-value finding before any expected inflammatory peak of pancreatitis; renal injury was accompanied by prominent urinary findings (hematuria and proteinuria) typical for hantavirus-mediated tubular injury rather than purely pre-renal renal impairment secondary to pancreatitis-related hypovolemia; and serum amylase/lipase remained within normal reference ranges throughout admission despite extensive peripancreatic exudates on CT imaging.The dynamic imaging feature observed in this case—progressive retroperitoneal exudation on contrast-enhanced CT accompanied by relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes—merits particular attention in the differential diagnosis of hantavirus infection presenting with abdominal manifestations. While AP is a recognized complication of HFRS, the typical CT findings in such cases commonly include pancreatic enlargement, peripancreatic edema, and occasionally necrosis or hemorrhage (4). However, extensive retroperitoneal involvement with a relatively preserved pancreatic gland reflects the underlying pathophysiological hallmark of hantavirus infection—virus-induced increased microvascular permeability leading to fluid extravasation into the retroperitoneal space. Indeed, the retroperitoneum has been identified as a major site of vascular leak in HFRS (11), and established evidence indicates that hantavirus elicits a robust inflammatory cascade with cytokine release and endothelial dysfunction that can produce extensive retroperitoneal fluid accumulation even in the absence of true pancreatic necrosis (12, 13). Prior case reports of HFRS mimicking acute pancreatitis have generally relied on single-time-point scans and could not capture this evolving radiological signature (7). Recognition of this distinctive pattern is of substantial practical importance, particularly in endemic regions (14, 15). From a clinical standpoint, progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic changes on follow-up CT, when accompanied by thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction, should prompt clinicians to broaden the differential beyond pancreatic pathology.Attributing the initial retroperitoneal exudation and abdominopelvic effusion to severe acute pancreatitis follows a conventional diagnostic pathway, given that such radiological findings are well-recognized features of this condition. However, the subsequent constellation of profound thrombocytopenia, progressive renal impairment, and urinary abnormalities extended beyond the typical scope of pancreatic pathology and prompted re-evaluation of the initial diagnostic assumption (9). This scenario illustrates a classic diagnostic pitfall, where an initially plausible diagnosis supported by compelling imaging can lead to anchoring bias that delays consideration of alternative etiologies with similar radiological features. Indeed, various infections mimic the clinical and radiological presentation of acute pancreatitis, including viral pathogens that also cause systemic thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction (16, 17); beyond pancreatitis, hantavirus infection can mimic other acute abdominal emergencies such as acute appendicitis (18, 19). Likewise, disproportionately low platelet counts without evidence of bone marrow suppression or disseminated intravascular coagulation have been emphasized as a key hematologic clue distinguishing HFRS from primary pancreatic or biliary etiologies (10, 20). Renal involvement manifesting as proteinuria and hematuria is a hallmark of orthohantavirus infection even in atypical presentations (10). The absence of gallstones, hypertriglyceridemia, or alcohol consumption—factors accounting for most acute pancreatitis cases—has likewise been underscored in previous reports of HFRS mimicking pancreatitis (4). Specifically, case reports and series have documented an association between hepatitis B and pancreatitis, although the pathogenic mechanism remains incompletely understood (23, 24). full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundHemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a zoonotic disease caused by orthohantaviruses, characterized by fever, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, and capillary leak syndrome. Its atypical presentations can closely mimic acute pancreatitis (AP), posing substantial diagnostic challenges.Case presentationA 33-year-old man presented with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. Initial computed tomography (CT) revealed peripancreatic and perirenal exudation suggestive of severe acute pancreatitis. He already had profound thrombocytopenia on admission (nadir 29 × 109/L), progressive renal impairment, hematuria, and proteinuria, without typical pancreatitis risk factors or elevated pancreatic enzymes. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated progressive retroperitoneal exudation with relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes and newly developed bilateral pleural effusion. Whole-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected high-copy Seoul orthohantavirus, with concurrent hepatitis B virus. The patient recovered fully with supportive care, intravenous immunoglobulin, and symptomatic treatment; pre-discharge ultrasound showed normal pancreatic morphology.ConclusionSeoul orthohantavirus infection can closely mimic severe acute pancreatitis clinically and radiologically. Disproportionate thrombocytopenia, renal involvement, and progressive retroperitoneal exudation with preserved pancreatic parenchyma are key diagnostic clues, and mNGS enables early definitive pathogen confirmation, facilitating appropriate management.

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis case highlights a diagnostically challenging presentation in which Seoul orthohantavirus infection clinically and radiologically mimicked severe acute pancreatitis, underscoring the need to consider HFRS in the differential diagnosis of unexplained pancreatitis-like presentations (1). Acute pancreatitis is a recognized but rare complication of HFRS (2, 6), and its distinction from hantavirus-induced pancreatic involvement is notoriously difficult because of overlapping clinical and imaging features (9). The present case further illustrates that peripancreatic exudation and retroperitoneal fluid—hallmark findings of severe acute pancreatitis—can also result from the profound systemic capillary leakage and retroperitoneal edema characteristic of hantavirus infection (4, 5). In this context, marked thrombocytopenia, renal impairment with hematuria and proteinuria, and the absence of typical pancreatitis risk factors constituted pivotal clues that prompted consideration of an alternative etiology (9). Moreover, the normal pancreatic enzyme levels observed here demonstrate that biochemical markers alone cannot reliably exclude HFRS in suspected pancreatitis (10).It should be acknowledged that severe acute pancreatitis itself may produce thrombocytopenia and renal dysfunction secondary to systemic inflammation. However, several features argued against primary acute pancreatitis in this patient: thrombocytopenia was already present at initial presentation as a critical-value finding before any expected inflammatory peak of pancreatitis; renal injury was accompanied by prominent urinary findings (hematuria and proteinuria) typical for hantavirus-mediated tubular injury rather than purely pre-renal renal impairment secondary to pancreatitis-related hypovolemia; and serum amylase/lipase remained within normal reference ranges throughout admission despite extensive peripancreatic exudates on CT imaging.The dynamic imaging feature observed in this case—progressive retroperitoneal exudation on contrast-enhanced CT accompanied by relatively mild pancreatic parenchymal changes—merits particular attention in the differential diagnosis of hantavirus infection presenting with abdominal manifestations. While AP is a recognized complication of HFRS, the typical CT findings in such cases commonly include pancreatic enlargement, peripancreatic edema, and occasionally necrosis or hemorrhage (4). However, extensive retroperitoneal involvement with a relatively preserved pancreatic gland reflects the underlying pathophysiological hallmark of hantavirus infection—virus-induced increased microvascular permeability leading to fluid extravasation into the retroperitoneal space. Indeed, the retroperitoneum has been identified as a major site of vascular leak in HFRS (11), and established evidence indicates that hantavirus elicits a robust inflammatory cascade with cytokine release and endothelial dysfunction that can produce extensive retroperitoneal fluid accumulation even in the absence of true pancreatic necrosis (12, 13). Prior case reports of HFRS mimicking acute pancreatitis have generally relied on single-time-point scans and could not capture this evolving radiological signature (7). Recognition of this distinctive pattern is of substantial practical importance, particularly in endemic regions (14, 15).
